summary: How US industrialists in the National Association of Manufacturers, led by J. Howard Pew, bankrolled minister James Fifield's Spiritual Mobilization from the 1930s to the 1950s to fuse Christianity with free-market opposition to the New Deal.
keywords: First Congregational Church of Los Angeles

evidence.note: Segment on socialist clergy backing the labor movement before the Depression
Depression and FDR's 1932 election push NAM into opposing the New Deal
Fifield addresses the NAM annual meeting in December 1940
Fifield takes over the indebted First Congregational Church of LA in 1935
NAM PR budget, school speakers bureau and canned editorials for newspapers
Pew and Crane introduced as the NAM men who back Fifield's approach
1950 Republican midterm gains credited to Spiritual Mobilization
1951 Committee to Proclaim Liberty and Freedom Under God Fourth of July events
Prayer Breakfast, under God in the Pledge, In God We Trust motto, 1953-1956
Fifield quits Spiritual Mobilization in 1957; Pew turns to Billy Graham
Pew-funded survey of Christianity Today readers, late 1950s
Closing on white evangelicals as the core of modern conservatism, sets reaches_present

notes: The primary subject is the movement, not Fifield, because the story is about the business campaign as a whole; Fifield's life is covered only from 1935, so making him primary would wrongly trigger the lifetime rule. The 1890s-1920s Christian socialists are treated as background. The Pew survey year is garbled in the transcript; read as 1958. reaches_present is borderline (Malheur pocket constitutions, evangelical voting shares).
